title: Perioperative hyperbaric oxygen therapy: mechanisms, evidence, and clinical application

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Perioperative hyperbaric oxygen therapy: mechanisms, evidence, and clinical application》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · sec1-p1】Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) delivers 100% oxygen at supra-atmospheric pressures within a sealed chamber, substantially increasing plasma oxygen content and tissue oxygen tension.1 Originally developed for decompression illness, HBOT has evolved into a versatile therapeutic tool for hypoxic, ischemic, and infectious conditions.1,2

【Introduction · sec1-p2】The perioperative period is divided into three phases: preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative (Figure 1).3 For this review, preoperative HBOT refers to treatments with the last session ≤ 72 hours before surgery, whereas postoperative HBOT refers to treatments initiated ≤ 2 weeks after surgery. HBOT administered during surgery would be considered intraoperative; however, we found no reports of intraoperative HBOT.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Perioperative hyperbaric oxygen therapy: mechanisms, evidence, and clinical application》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Design Limitations · sec19-p3】Additionally, most available studies are small, single-center, or observational, and are often limited due to chamber availability and patient selection bias. Future work should consist of adequately powered, multicenter, protocol-harmonized trials that prioritize early initiation and standardized surgical endpoints (graft/flap salvage, necrosis rates, re-operation, time-to-ambulation, and perioperative quality of life). Additional gaps include optimal timing relative to surgery for each procedure (preconditioning vs. complication management) and establishing minimum effective pressures and session numbers.

【Methods · sec2-p1】We performed a narrative literature review to synthesize clinical evidence on perioperative HBOT. MEDLINE, PubMed and, when available, Embase and the Cochrane Library, were searched from inception to December 31, 2025, and reference lists of relevant reviews and high-yield primary studies were hand-searched to identify additional articles. Search terms combined keywords and controlled vocabulary for HBOT and perioperative surgery (e.g., “hyperbaric oxygen,” “HBOT,” “perioperative,” “preoperative,” “intraoperative,” “postoperative,” “surgery,” “reconstruction,” “flap,” “graft,” “ischemia-reperfusion,” “radiation injury,” “orthopedic”), with database-specific adaptations. In addition to database searching, we used artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted discovery tools (ChatGPT in Deep Research mode and the browser version) to identify potentially relevant articles not found with keyword searches. All AI-suggested records were treated only as leads and were independently screened. Articles were included if the relevant study population met criteria for perioperative HBOT as defined in the introduction and the study reported at least one clinically relevant outcome. Articles were excluded if they were not published in English.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Perioperative hyperbaric oxygen therapy: mechanisms, evidence, and clinical application》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · sec20-p1】Perioperative HBOT represents an evolving intersection between surgical innovation and translational physiology. Decades of evidence demonstrate that oxygen is not merely a passive substrate, but a molecule capable of regulating inflammation, angiogenesis, and cellular repair. With strategic administration around the time of surgery, HBOT has shown potential to enhance these processes at precisely the stage when tissues are most susceptible to hypoxia and reperfusion injury (Figure 2). HBOT improves blood flow, supports tissue healing, and reduces infection risk, with relatively few safety concerns, making it a promising option in perioperative care.

【Conclusion · sec20-p2】Across surgical disciplines, the most consistent evidence demonstrates that the timing of HBOT is a key predictor of effectiveness. Early initiation appears to confer the most significant benefit, improving wound perfusion, graft adherence, and functional recovery. Interpretation of this literature is constrained by the narrative design of this review, which did not employ a preregistered systematic search strategy or uniform risk-of-bias adjudication across all included studies. Moreover, the underlying clinical evidence is heterogeneous in indications, HBOT dosing and timing, co-interventions, and outcome definitions, and is dominated in several domains by small trials and nonrandomized designs that remain vulnerable to confounding and publication bias. Nonetheless, the aggregate evidence supports HBOT as a potentially valuable adjunct when applied early and selectively in high-risk or ischemic perioperative settings.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Perioperative hyperbaric oxygen therapy: mechanisms, evidence, and clinical application》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Figure 1 · mgr.MEDGASRES-D-25-00318-F1】Figure 1 Timing and dose–response framework for perioperative hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT).Initiation soon after surgery or at the first signs of flap/graft compromise is most likely to enhance I/R protection, support perfusion-dependent healing (e.g., graft uptake/flap viability), and temper inflammation. Benefit declines with delay, as established necrosis, infection, or microvascular failure becomes less reversible and more dependent on operative revision and source control. The figure separates late postoperative/salvage use (> 2 weeks) as a setting where HBOT may still help selected patients, especially when chronic hypoxia or radiation-related microvascular injury constrains healing, but with generally less predictable benefit than early perioperative initiation. Created with Microsoft PowerPoint for Mac (version 16.83). ATA: Atmospheres absolute; BID: twice daily; HBOT: hyperbaric oxygen therapy; I/R: ischemia–reperfusion.

【Figure 2 · mgr.MEDGASRES-D-25-00318-F2】Figure 2 Mechanism of perioperative hyperbaric oxygen therapy.Exposure to 100% oxygen at supra-atmospheric pressures (2.0–3.0 ATA) increases plasma-dissolved and tissue pO2, enabling oxygen diffusion beyond hemoglobin-dependent perfusion. This hyperoxic exposure induces a controlled, transient oxidative signal that activates redox-sensitive pathways, including HIF-1α–mediated angiogenic signaling (e.g., VEGF), Nrf2-dependent antioxidant defenses (e.g., SOD, catalase, GPx), and nitric oxide-dependent mobilization of CD34+ progenitor cells. At the microcirculatory level, HBOT reduces erythrocyte aggregation and increases red blood cell deformability, improving capillary transit while oxygen-induced vasoconstriction limits tissue edema without compromising oxygen delivery. Concurrent immunologic and antimicrobial effects include attenuation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), inhibition of neutrophil β2-integrin adhesion with reduced I/R injury, enhancement of polymorphonuclear leukocyte oxidative burst, and potentiation of select antimicrobial agents. Collectively, these integrated mechanisms promote angiogenesis and collagen deposition, reduce I/R–related necrosis, and improve wound closure and graft or flap survival in the perioperative setting. Created with Microsoft PowerPoint for Mac (version 16.83). ATA: Atmospheres absolute; GPx: glutathione peroxidase; HBOT: hyperbaric oxygen therapy; HIF-1α: hypoxia-inducible factor-1α; I/R: ischemia–reperfusion; IL: interleukin; Nrf2: nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2; PMN: polymorphonuclear leukocyte; pO2: oxygen tension; RBC: red blood cell; SOD: superoxide dismutase; TNF-α: tumor necrosis factor-α; VEGF: vascular endothelial growth factor.

【Figure 3 · mgr.MEDGASRES-D-25-00318-F3】Figure 3 Evidence of perioperative HBOT by surgical domain.The most consistent clinical benefit of perioperative HBOT is observed when therapy is initiated early in ischemic or hypoperfused tissues, particularly for reducing necrosis and enhancing tissue viability, while also highlighting persistent limitations related to protocol heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and incomplete standardization across surgical specialties. Rows represent surgical contexts (trauma surgery; orthopedic and musculoskeletal surgery; reconstructive and oncologic surgery; radiation-injured or ischemic tissue reconstruction; cardiovascular surgery), and columns represent clinically relevant outcomes, including soft-tissue necrosis or ischemic loss, infection or wound complications, graft or flap survival, functional or muscle recovery, and length of stay or ICU metrics. Cell color denotes the overall direction of effect reported in the literature: green, benefit demonstrated; gray, mixed or insufficient evidence; red, no benefit or adverse signal. Created with Microsoft PowerPoint for Mac (version 16.83). HBOT: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy; ICU: intensive care unit; RCT: randomized controlled trial.
